implementation_notes: The rules are ordinary strongly typed options bound from configuration, and IOptionsMonitor re-materialises them when a provider reports a change, so reading .CurrentValue once per message yields a consistent, reloadable rule set (IOptions freezes at startup and IOptionsSnapshot is scoped). Destinations are resolved from a registry - a dictionary of delegates, keyed DI services, or a channel or queue name - and a missing key must go to an explicit dead-letter destination. Subscribe with OnChange when a new rule set needs validation or logging at the moment it lands.
pitfalls: IOptions<T> is a singleton whose value is computed once: a router injecting it silently ignores every later rule edit - use IOptionsMonitor or IOptionsSnapshot.

Change notifications only come from providers that report them (file-based providers do; a rule push over the network does not), so a pushed rule set needs an explicit IOptionsMonitorCache<T>.TryRemove invalidation.
Reading CurrentValue inside a per-message loop re-runs the options pipeline; read it once and pass the snapshot down.

variants.name: WCF Routing Service filter table with ApplyConfiguration
variants.implementation_notes: The classic .NET realization is WCF's Routing Service: a MessageFilterTable maps MessageFilter implementations (address, action, XPath, match-all, or a custom filter) to destination endpoint lists, and the documented runtime update path is to build a new RoutingConfiguration and hand it to RoutingExtension.ApplyConfiguration, which lets in-flight messages finish on the previous configuration. Filters can carry priorities (highest priority level wins, lower levels are not evaluated) and each entry can list backup endpoints used when a transmission to the primary fails. Prefer it when the traffic is SOAP/WCF-shaped and the router is a service rather than an application component.
pitfalls: RouteOnHeadersOnly defaults to true, so content-based filters silently never see the message body until it is set to false.
Only ApplyConfiguration is a supported runtime mutation: editing RoutingConfiguration.FilterTable after start has no effect and is not atomic.
Backup endpoint lists only cover transmission failures, so a wrong rule can flood the fallback instead of surfacing an error.
